blurbs.text: NASA's Artemis program is taking astronauts back to the Moon — for the first time since the 1970s! These missions test the rocket, the capsule, and everything needed to build a permanent Moon base.
blurbs.title: Back to the Moon!

blurbs.text: SpaceX's Starship is the biggest rocket ever built — taller than the Statue of Liberty! Each test flight teaches engineers something new. One day Starship is supposed to carry people to the Moon and Mars.
blurbs.title: The Giant Test Rocket

blurbs.text: This is a delivery run to the International Space Station! The capsule carries food, clothes, spare parts, and brand-new science experiments for the astronauts living and working up there.
blurbs.title: Groceries for the Space Station

blurbs.text: People are riding this rocket! Astronauts are heading to a space station to live and work in orbit — doing science experiments and taking care of the station for months at a time.
blurbs.title: Astronauts On Board!

blurbs.text: These satellites join the Starlink constellation, beaming internet down to places on Earth where cables and cell towers can't reach — remote towns, ships at sea, and airplanes.
blurbs.title: Internet From Space

blurbs.text: Amazon's Kuiper satellites are building another space-internet network, bringing fast connections to homes, schools, and villages that don't have good internet yet.
blurbs.title: Internet From Space

blurbs.text: Rocket Lab's Electron is a small, speedy rocket that launches small satellites — the kind built by universities and small companies. Small rockets mean more teams get to go to space!
blurbs.title: The Little Rocket That Could

blurbs.text: New Glenn is Blue Origin's giant reusable rocket. Its first stages are designed to land back on a ship and fly again — reuse is what makes spaceflight cheaper over time.
blurbs.title: Blue Origin's Big Rocket

blurbs.text: United Launch Alliance rockets carry important cargo: military satellites that keep countries safe, science missions, and sometimes probes heading to other planets.
blurbs.title: America's Workhorse

blurbs.text: Europe's Ariane rocket launches satellites for weather forecasting, TV, internet, and science — including missions built by the European Space Agency.
blurbs.title: Europe's Ride to Space

blurbs.text: Japan's H3 rocket is carrying a mission to study the moons of Mars! Learning about other worlds helps scientists understand how our whole solar system formed.
blurbs.title: Japan's Moon Explorer

blurbs.text: This mission is flying to Phobos, one of Mars's two tiny moons, to scoop up a sample and bring it home to Earth. Scientists want to know: where did these moons come from?
blurbs.title: Visiting the Moons of Mars

blurbs.text: These are Earth-watching satellites. They take pictures and radar scans of our planet to track weather, ships, forests, and changes on the ground — day and night.
blurbs.title: Eyes on Earth

blurbs.text: Navigation satellites are the reason your family's phone knows exactly where you are. This launch adds another one to the sky's GPS network.
blurbs.title: The Satellites That Find You

blurbs.text: Weather satellites stare at Earth around the clock, tracking hurricanes, storms, and wildfires so forecasters can warn people in time. This launch puts a new watcher on duty.
blurbs.title: Weather Watchers

blurbs.text: Space telescopes see things no Earth telescope can — distant galaxies, newborn stars, and planets around other suns. This mission adds a powerful new eye in the sky.
blurbs.title: A New Eye on the Universe

blurbs.text: China launches rockets often — carrying satellites, space station parts for Tiangong, and science missions. Their program is one of the busiest in the world.
blurbs.title: China's Space Program

blurbs.text: India's space agency is famous for doing big missions on small budgets — including landing near the Moon's south pole! This launch adds satellites for navigation and science.
blurbs.title: India's Space Program

blurbs.text: This Chinese rocket burns methane fuel — the same kind of fuel SpaceX's Starship uses. Methane engines could be refueled on Mars one day, which is why engineers are excited about them.
blurbs.title: A Methane-Powered Rocket

blurbs.text: Rideshare missions are like carpools for satellites! Lots of small satellites from different teams share one rocket, which makes getting to space much cheaper for everyone.
blurbs.title: The Carpool to Space

blurbs.text: This satellite helps keep a country safe — watching for missile launches, guiding troops, or carrying secure communications. Space is part of how nations protect themselves.
blurbs.title: Guardians of the Sky

default.text: A rocket is heading to space carrying satellites or science cargo. Every launch teaches engineers something new — and every one brings the future a little closer.
default.title: Up, Up, and Away!
